name: Disagree Then Commit
definition: After a decision is made, we expect everyone, including the people who argued for a different approach, to disagree then commit. This helps ensure the outcome is as successful as possible.

rows.situation: A decision that went against the approach you argued for
rows.under: Relitigates it in side conversations, or complies so slowly that it fails.
rows.justRight: Commits. You carry the decision as if you wanted the outcome to work, because you do.
rows.over: Pretends you agreed all along, so the next decision never hears the dissent you actually had.

rows.situation: Explaining the decision to people who know you disagreed
rows.under: Signals that you are only going along, and invites them to drag their feet.
rows.justRight: Explains the decision cleanly, including that you had argued the other way, and asks for the same commitment.
rows.over: Gives a speech about your loyalty and does not do the work the decision requires.

rows.situation: Your team preferred a path the captain did not pick
rows.under: Lets the team keep building the path that lost.
rows.justRight: Switches the team to the chosen path and removes the ambiguity about which one is real.
rows.over: Shuts down every question about how to implement, and calls that commitment.

rows.situation: The hour the decision is actually made
rows.under: Keeps a private veto for a few more days.
rows.justRight: The disagreeing stops when the decision is made, unless a genuinely new fact appears.
rows.over: Treats the decision as sacred even after a new fact makes it harmful.

rows.situation: Work you still think is the second-best path
rows.under: Does the minimum and waits to be proved right.
rows.justRight: Puts real effort into making the chosen path succeed.
rows.over: Over-invests in proving the decision was wise, and hides the early signs it was not.
